title: James Webb Space Telescope: Peering into the Cosmic Dawn
source_book: The James Webb Space Telescope: Science Guide and First Deep Field (NASA / ESA / CSA)
source_chapter: First Images from the James Webb Space Telescope (SMACS 0723)

content:
On Christmas morning, December 25, 2021, an Ariane 5 rocket roared into the skies above the European Spaceport in French Guiana. Packed inside its tight 5.4-meter nose fairing was humanity's most complex and audacious scientific machine: the **James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)**.

Thirty years in development, Webb was built to succeed the legendary Hubble Space Telescope. But where Hubble viewed the universe primarily in visible light, Webb was designed to see in the **infrared**.

Because the universe has been expanding for 13.8 billion years, light emitted by the very first stars and galaxies has been stretched by cosmological redshift all the way from visible wavelengths into the long, invisible infrared. Furthermore, infrared light effortlessly pierces through dense curtains of cosmic dust that blind optical telescopes.

To detect these faint heat whispers from the dawn of time, Webb had to operate in deep, unimaginable cold: below -233°C (-388°F).

Webb journeyed one million miles (1.5 million kilometers) away from Earth to **Lagrange Point 2 (L2)**. Over a month of breathless tension, flight controllers orchestrated a sequence of 344 'single-point-of-failure' deployments: unfurling a five-layer Kapton sunshield the size of a tennis court to block the heat of the Sun, Earth, and Moon, followed by locking eighteen hexagonal beryllium mirrors coated in microscopic pure gold into a single 6.5-meter giant honeycomb eye.

On July 11, 2022, the world held its collective breath as the White House unveiled **Webb's First Deep Field** (SMACS 0723).

Covering a patch of sky no larger than a grain of sand held at arm's length by someone on the ground, the image blazed with thousands of galaxies. Foreground galaxy clusters acted as a colossal cosmic magnifying glass (gravitational lensing), warping distant background light into glowing streaks and revealing galaxies that blazed more than 13.1 billion years ago—just after the Big Bang!

From Archimedes in Syracuse to the golden mirrors of Webb at L2, humanity's quest to decipher the book of nature had crossed millennia. The journey of scientific discovery was not ending; it had only just begun.

stem_vocabulary.definition: A gravitationally stable position in space roughly 1.5 million kilometers behind Earth where a satellite stays in sync with Earth's orbit around the Sun.
A branch of astronomy that studies astronomical objects visible in infrared (IR) radiation, piercing interstellar dust clouds.
The bending and magnification of light from distant background galaxies by the immense gravity of a foreground galaxy cluster.
The epoch in the early universe, roughly 100 to 500 million years after the Big Bang, when the first stars and galaxies ignited.
